echoes.note: Tertullus and the elders bring formal, hostile charges against Paul before the governor; the situation of the righteous man delivered up to the will of false, violent accusers echoes the psalmist's cry against 'false witnesses' who 'breathe out cruelty.' Thematically coherent with the Lukan figural pattern of the just sufferer hauled before rulers; verbal volume is low, so echo rather than allusion.

'Malicious witnesses rise up; they ask me of things I know not.' The hired orator's manufactured indictment ('a plague,' 'instigator of insurrections,' temple-profaner) fits the lament topos of the innocent assailed by lying accusers. Recurs across Luke-Acts; no direct quotation, hence echo.

Paul is denounced as ringleader of 'the sect of the Nazarenes.' The title Nazarene is widely traced to the messianic netzer ('branch') of Isaiah's stump-of-Jesse oracle; the accusation thus carries, ironically, a hidden scriptural-messianic claim. Contested and indirect, voiced by opponents, so low confidence.

'Wicked and deceitful mouths are opened against me... they encircle me with words of hatred.' The choreographed, flattering-then-accusing speech of Tertullus, joined by the assembled Jews, resonates with the imprecatory lament against encircling slanderers. Faint, no shared diction.

Paul stresses he went up 'to worship at Jerusalem' only days before, a pious pilgrim, not an agitator; the pilgrimage-to-Zion frame faintly recalls the Songs of Ascents ('let us go to the house of the LORD'). Thematic only, no verbal borrowing.

'Nor can they prove to you the things of which they accuse me' anticipates Paul's evidentiary appeal; the Deuteronomic rule that a charge stands only on established proof / multiple witnesses underlies his demand. Developed more fully in 24:19; here only incipient, hence low.

Paul confesses he serves 'the God of our fathers' (ho theos ton pateron), the covenant self-designation given at the burning bush, 'the God of your fathers... my memorial to all generations.' High thematic coherence and recurrent formula; standard Septuagintal idiom Paul deliberately claims to assert continuity, not novelty.

'There will be a resurrection of the dead, both of the just and unjust' closely tracks Daniel's 'many who sleep in the dust shall awake, some to everlasting life and some to shame and everlasting contempt' — the locus classicus for a two-fold resurrection of righteous and wicked. High volume and thematic coherence; the bifurcation just/unjust is distinctively Danielic.

'Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise... the earth will give birth to the dead.' Paul's hope of bodily resurrection draws on this prophetic resurrection text alongside Daniel; supports the claim that his hope rests on 'the law and the prophets.' Medium: real thematic match, less verbal proximity than Daniel.

'We cried to the LORD, the God of our fathers' — the credal recital tying worship to the ancestral God reinforces Paul's 'God of our fathers' framing as covenant fidelity. Faint, overlaps with the Exodus 3:15 idiom.

'They ought to have been here before you, and to make accusation' — Paul invokes the legal principle that accusers must appear and a charge requires proper witnesses; the absent Asian Jews cannot satisfy the Deuteronomic requirement. Coherent with Mosaic judicial procedure; medium.

Paul was 'found purified in the temple' with offerings; this reflects completion of a Nazirite-style vow of purification (cf. Acts 21:23-26), the rite of Numbers 6 requiring offerings at the sanctuary. Concrete ritual referent; medium.
Paul came 'to bring gifts for the needy to my nation' — almsgiving to the poor reflects the Torah's command to open the hand to the needy. Thematic, no verbal link.

Paul reiterates that he is on trial 'concerning the resurrection of the dead,' recurring to the same Danielic hope voiced in 24:15; recurrence within the chapter strengthens the link. Echo here since the topic is named without restating the just/unjust formula.

Felix keeps Paul in custody but grants him privileges and freedom to receive his friends — the imprisoned righteous man shown favor while detained typologically recalls Joseph, to whom the LORD gave favor in the prison-keeper's sight. No verbal borrowing; figural pattern of the just one preserved in confinement.

As Paul reasons about righteousness, self-control, and the coming judgment, the ruler Felix 'was terrified' — recalling Belshazzar, before whom the prophetic word made the king's countenance change and his knees knock. The motif of God's spokesman striking dread into a powerful but compromised ruler is typologically apt; medium for thematic coherence.

Paul's reasoning about 'the judgment to come' echoes Qoheleth's conclusion that 'God will bring every deed into judgment, with every secret thing, whether good or evil.' Coherent with the eschatological-accountability theme that unsettles Felix; medium.

Felix 'hoped that money would be given to him by Paul' — a corrupt judge angling for a bribe stands in direct contrast to the Torah's prohibition, 'You shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of the righteous.' Felix embodies the very corruption the law forbids; medium thematic coherence.

Paul preaching righteousness and judgment to the cohabiting Felix and Drusilla (Felix's union with a Jewess he had taken) recalls the prophet confronting a ruler over righteousness and unlawful marriage, as Nathan confronted David ('You are the man'). Figural pattern of bold prophetic confrontation; low, no diction.
